title: A House for the Smile
premise: Folklorist Astrid Ashgrove arrives in the fog-bound village of Hollowmere to record its songs, only to find every tune must be sung twice—once for the living, once for something the villagers won't name. Her overnight sleep recordings capture a second voice answering her questions, a thing that has been waiting beneath the village well since a drowned girl was denied justice generations ago. As Astrid pieces together the truth—that the village's founding families invited the entity in as an executioner and have fed it silence ever since—the house she lodges in begins counting doors that aren't there. In the final hours before sunrise, Astrid must choose between fleeing and singing the forbidden song herself, giving the drowned girl a name and a verdict, which frees the village but binds the debt to Astrid's own memory.
about_author: Xanthe Nystrom is the pen name of a former archivist of oral histories who spent years collecting lullabies in coastal settlements before turning to fiction. They write horror about what communities agree not to remember, and live somewhere with too many doors.

chapters.title: The Village That Sings Everything Twice
chapters.summary: Astrid arrives in Hollowmere by last ferry, recording equipment in hand, and is met by landlady Maren Voss who warns them never to ask why every song ends twice. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity masked as professional detachment.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Settling into the lodging house, Astrid catalogs eleven doors but finds twelve hinges; Maren insists the twelfth was bricked over 'for reasons of tidiness.' POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: creeping wrongness beneath domestic routine.

chapters.title: The Song Nobody Will Sing Twice
chapters.summary: At the tavern, fiddler Old Bram performs a lament and stops mid-refusal when asked to repeat it; the room goes silent and drinks are poured without speaking. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: first open wound in the village's polite surface.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Hears at Night
chapters.summary: Reviewing overnight sleep recordings, Astrid hears their own murmured questions—and a second voice, wet and patient, answering each one correctly. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: cold shock; the professional becomes the subject.

chapters.title: Maren's Version of History
chapters.summary: Astrid probes Maren about the parish records; Maren offers a scrubbed history of a mill flood and a girl named Ilse who 'wasn't mourned properly,' then begs Astrid to leave before the equinox. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: pity tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: The Well That Answers
chapters.summary: Astrid visits the capped well behind the chapel and drops a recorder on a string; the playback returns their own voice asking questions they don't remember asking. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: vertigo—the boundary between self and other blurring.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession Over Cheap Whiskey
chapters.summary: Old Bram, drunk, admits the founding families made a bargain: the thing under the well punishes the guilty so no court ever has to, and it demands the second singing as payment. POV: Bram. Emotional beat: guilt finally cracking open.

chapters.title: Ilse Had a Name
chapters.summary: In the flooded church archive, Astrid finds Ilse Brandt's true record: drowned by four respected men who were never tried, her song banned from repetition to keep her from being remembered. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: righteous anger igniting.

chapters.title: The House Begins Counting Back
chapters.summary: The lodging house starts responding—doors Astrid counts aloud are answered by knocks, one more each night, until the tally exceeds the walls. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: terror of being measured by something patient.

chapters.title: They Knew You Were Coming
chapters.summary: Astrid discovers their arrival was arranged: a letter in Maren's hand invited 'a listener' months ago; the village didn't want songs recorded—they wanted someone to hear the answer. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: betrayal and dawning purpose.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Has Questions Too
chapters.summary: That night the recording captures the entity asking Astrid questions—about justice, about names, about whether the living deserve silence—and waits through the static for answers. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: horrifying intimacy; it wants a verdict, not a victim.

chapters.title: Descendants of the Four
chapters.summary: Astrid identifies the four founders' living descendants, including Maren, whose family line traces directly to the man who held Ilse under. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: moral weight shifting onto the innocent-seeming.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: The village prepares for the equinox with candles and locked doors; children are told stories about tides, and everyone pretends the extra knocking isn't happening. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: communal dread and complicity.

chapters.title: The Twelfth Door Opens
chapters.summary: At midnight the bricked-over door unbricks itself from inside; Astrid follows the sound down stairs that shouldn't exist beneath the lodging house toward water and lamplight. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: crossing the threshold past retreat.

chapters.title: Under the Well
chapters.summary: Below, Astrid meets the drowned girl—not a monster but a kept thing, still wearing the shape of the night she died, reciting the names of the guilty for two hundred years. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: grief displacing fear.

chapters.title: The Bargain Explained
chapters.summary: The entity explains the terms: it holds the village safe from all other harm in exchange for the second singing and its prison of silence; end the song, end the protection, end the punishment—or finish it. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: the trap of justice outside the law.

chapters.title: Sunrise Is a Deadline
chapters.summary: Astrid climbs back up to find the village gathered with lanterns, demanding they leave before dawn; Maren confesses the invitation and begs forgiveness she can't define. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: shame meeting accountability.

chapters.title: The Trial Nobody Called
chapters.summary: Astrid forces the descendants to hear the recordings—Ilse's name, the four confessions preserved in the well's echo—as the house counts down doors like a clock. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: improvised justice, terrifying and necessary.

chapters.title: Sing It Twice
chapters.summary: As the sky grays, Astrid sings Ilse's lament alone, then sings it again—the first true second singing in two centuries—and the whole village, weeping, joins on the repeat. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: catharsis; grief given its voice.

chapters.title: The Verdict Below
chapters.summary: The entity delivers its final judgment: the guilty lines are marked, the innocent freed, and Ilse released—but the debt of hearing must pass to whoever listened longest. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: sacrifice accepted with clear eyes.

chapters.title: What Astrid Forgot on Purpose
chapters.summary: Sunrise comes; the well is quiet, the twelfth door is brick again, and Astrid wakes unable to recall their mother's face—the price paid willingly. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: bittersweet loss traded for a village's freedom.

chapters.title: Coda: The Ferryman's Question
chapters.summary: Leaving on the morning ferry, Astrid records one last track: a new song, sung once, left unfinished—because some things should wait for a second voice. POV: Astrid. Emotional beat: haunted peace; the story continues beyond the page.
